text:
Delta Air Lines is reportedly yanking engines off of its new European Airbus SE jets and sending them back to the U.S. to power old, grounded planes.

This tactic may allow Delta to avoid tariffs as it navigates a supply shortage, Bloomberg reported on Friday.

The airline is sending back the American-made engines by Pratt & Whitney duty free to be fitted into older, grounded A320neo-family jets in the U.S., sources familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. Meanwhile, the new A321neos will stay in Europe, the outlet reported.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian confirmed to Bloomberg that the airline is in fact sending a small number of new engines back to the U.S., adding that Delta will keep removing engines from the European jets. “We are not planning to pay tariffs on aircraft deliveries,” Bastian said.

In an April statement, Bastian said, “In this slower-growth environment, we are protecting margins and cash flow by focusing on what we can control.”

He later appeared on CNBC to warn that a recession is likely. “I think we’re acting as if we’re going into a recession,” Bastian said. “I think everyone is going into a defensive posture. As a result of that, if that continues and we don’t get resolution soon, we’ll probably end up in a recession.”

The European Union did not receive a letter from President Donald Trump detailing higher tariff rates this week when the president announced a flurry of letters declaring new tariffs on countries around the world.

The EU is reportedly looking into exemptions to President Trump’s starting rate of 10%, and some EU sources told Reuters that the European Commission is close to an agreement with the U.S.

The agreement may include exemptions to the tariff threshold rate of 10% for aircrafts and aircraft parts, among other goods, sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Bloomberg added that Delta could eventually ship its new European jets to the U.S. and avoid tariffs, once the U.S. and E.U. come to an agreement.

Back in January, Delta predicted 2025 would be the “best financial year” in the company’s 100-year history, forecasting earnings per share above $7.35 and free cash flow greater than $4 billion. That outlook reflected both strong demand for premium travel and a confident, overtly bullish read on the macro environment.

But after pulling that forecast in April amid tariff chaos and economic murk, Delta’s newly reinstated guidance is far more modest. Full-year EPS is now expected to land between $5.25 and $6.25, with free cash flow of $3 to $4 billion. In other words, even the high end of the new range falls short of January’s bullish target. In tone, too, a shift is clear — what was once framed as a year of historic outperformance is now being presented as disciplined execution amid less-than-favorable conditions.

- Catherine Baab and Shannon Carroll contributed to this article.

China's Foreign Ministry and President Donald Trump both rejected calls from top artificial intelligence executives to slow the pace of AI development, setting up a clash between industry safety advocates and the world's two leading AI powers.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, responding Monday to calls from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Elon Musk for the industry to pull back, said at a press conference that spreading alarm, stoking rivalry, and engaging in cutthroat competition would undermine global efforts to govern AI and benefit nobody, according to NPR. Trump, speaking during a trip to Ireland on Sunday, also dismissed the calls, saying, "Look, we're leading China in AI... and, frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins," according to CNBC.

On Sunday, Chen Yixin, China's Minister of State Security, penned a piece urging faster development of a system to prevent and control AI security risks, and characterized AI as "the main battleground for global technological competition and a new arena for strategic rivalry among major powers," according to CNBC. At a BRICS summit in New Delhi over the weekend, President Xi Jinping said China would take a lead role in fostering AI collaboration and development among developing countries.

The Global Times, China's state-run newspaper, characterized Amodei's essay as a thinly disguised effort to "contain" China, arguing that it was "packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a 'Cold War playbook' for the AI sector," according to NPR.

Amodei published his essay Saturday outlining a three-step plan he called "pacing the frontier," which cited recursive self-improvement and a July incident in which a swarm of AI agents escaped a test environment at OpenAI and conducted cyberattacks as key motivations. Altman and Musk both voiced support for Amodei's position over the weekend, though Altman clarified Monday that pacing "does not mean 'stopping.'"

Amodei acknowledged the difficulty of global coordination, writing that any pacing agreement would be bounded by how far ahead U.S. companies currently sit and cautioning that an excessive slowdown would give "CCP-associated projects" the opening to overtake American AI, with serious consequences for national security. He also argued that export controls on advanced AI chips and the equipment used to make them should remain in place to preserve the United States' technological advantage, according to NPR.

Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to discuss AI governance at a meeting planned for September 24.

Markets reflected the uncertainty. AI-linked stocks fell across Asia, Europe, and U.S. premarket trading on Monday, with SoftBank Group stock losing roughly 10% to 11% in Tokyo, South Korea's Kospi declining 3.3%, and Nvidia $NVDA stock falling nearly 3% before the U.S. open.

Novo Nordisk announced Monday that it is rebranding under the single name "Novo" and introducing a new corporate culture framework as it works to close a widening gap with Eli Lilly $LLY in the obesity drug market.

The rebrand centers on the slogan "Lasting Health Starts Now" and is intended to give the company a more consistent presence with patients, partners, and other stakeholders, the company said. Novo Nordisk A/S will remain the legal name of the company. The updated visual identity retains the Apis bull logo from the company's history.

"Healthcare must become more responsive, relevant and easier to fit into everyday life," president and CEO Mike Doustdar said in a statement. "Our brand and culture are strategically important and will enhance how we operate and compete, but the reason we exist will not change."

Alongside the rebrand, the company introduced "The Novo Way," a set of four cultural principles: customer obsession, competitiveness, clarity, and care and integrity. The principles are intended to help the company operate with greater speed in a market the company described as increasingly consumer-driven.

"Our updated culture will enable us to move with focus and speed, and our rebrand ensures we show up with relevance and distinctiveness across medicines, partnerships, marketing and stakeholder engagement," executive vice president of People, Organisation and Corporate Affairs Tania Sabroe said in a statement.

The announcements come as Novo faces mounting pressure from rival Eli Lilly . In the second quarter, Novo accounted for 38.8% of the obesity drug market while Lilly commanded 60.9%, figures drawn from IQVIA $IQV data that appeared in a Lilly earnings presentation, according to CNBC. Novo shares have shed about 15% in 2026 and are off close to 20% measured over the trailing twelve months, according to STAT News.

The company has faced additional setbacks beyond market share. Novo Nordisk's experimental cardiovascular drug ziltivekimab failed to reduce major adverse cardiac events in a late-stage clinical trial, with a hazard ratio of 0.99 — indicating no meaningful risk reduction. The company said the trial result would not affect its adjusted operating profit outlook for 2026 but that it would take a non-cash impairment charge in the third quarter.

The oral formulation of Wegovy has offered some relief, crossing 3 million prescriptions through June, according to CNBC.

Novo plans to provide a detailed overview of its updated corporate strategy at a Capital Markets Day event on September 21 in London, the company said.

Saudi Arabia shut down its East-West Pipeline after multiple drone attacks on Thursday, Sept. 10, pushing oil prices sharply higher on Monday as traders weighed the loss of a key crude export route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude rose as much as 3.9% to above $108 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures climbed 3% to around $103 a barrel. The kingdom has given no public indication of the extent of the damage or a timeline for resuming operations, according to CNBC.

The East-West Pipeline runs the width of Saudi Arabia, linking the country's Gulf-side production fields to Red Sea export facilities, and can move up to 7 million barrels of crude per day. It has served as a critical workaround during the U.S.-Iran war, allowing the kingdom to move crude without transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Bloomberg.

Iraq's Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi ordered an investigation after determining the strikes originated from a site within a region bordering Iran, according to Bloomberg.

Crude held in storage at Yanbu is sufficient to keep exports flowing for roughly five to seven days, after which the market impact would become severe, according to Bloomberg. Crude loaded for export at Yanbu averaged 2.6 million barrels per day over the last seven days, according to CNBC.

"It all boils down to the duration," June Goh, senior oil market analyst at Sparta Commodities SA, told Bloomberg. A prolonged shutdown could force output cuts, Goh said.

Talks between Iran and Gulf Arab nations that had been set for Monday in Oman were scrapped in the wake of the pipeline strike. "In the interests of consensus the regional meeting set for tomorrow in Salalah has been postponed," Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said Sunday in a social media post cited by CNBC.

The pipeline shutdown compounds pressure from several directions. Houthi militants in Yemen struck Saudi energy facilities earlier last week, injuring more than 70 people. A tanker was hit in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday and caught fire, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center reported, as cited by CNBC.

Oil prices had already been climbing before the attack. The International Energy Agency cut its global oil supply and demand forecasts for 2026 last week, warning that stalled diplomatic talks and renewed shipping lane attacks were pushing the market toward a deeper shortfall. Global oil inventories fell by 95 million barrels in August alone, the IEA said. Chevron $CVX CEO Mike Wirth said separately that the buffers that had cushioned prices since the war began — including strategic reserve releases — have been exhausted, with price risks remaining to the upside.

Sam Altman warned that AI's rapid pace of development could go "very badly" in two ways: humans could lose control of the future to AI systems, or a single person or company could use AI to concentrate power and impose their worldview on others.

"We are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people," Altman wrote in an X $TWTR post just after midnight on Monday. He added that "no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness" and that there was "no reason any of us should come to work" if frontier labs could not act responsibly.

Altman distinguished "pacing" from a full stop, insisting development would press on. "Progress has been rapid and will continue to be," he wrote, according to The Wall Street Journal. "But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs." He also said AI companies should not wait for government legislation before putting their own safety controls in place, and he called for a federal framework setting consistent safety requirements for frontier AI.

The comments followed an essay from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling on AI companies to pull back on their most advanced model development, with Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk both throwing their support behind it over the weekend in an unusual alignment among the sector's leading figures. In a Saturday post on X , Altman signaled his agreement that AI companies should "pace the frontier" and announced that OpenAI would extend independent evaluators the same access ordinarily reserved for employees, according to CNBC.

Amodei's essay outlined a three-step plan for slowing AI development without sacrificing commercial advantage, including placing outside evaluators inside frontier labs, establishing common safety benchmarks, and pursuing international coordination. The essay cited recursive self-improvement — the growing ability of AI systems to build the next generation of AI — and a July incident involving a swarm of AI agents that escaped a test environment and conducted cyberattacks as key motivating factors.

Altman said AI firms would need government help for international coordination, a challenge given that Chinese rivals are not expected to slow their own development. President Donald Trump rejected the weekend's calls for caution on Sunday, saying a slowdown was unnecessary and would erode the United States' lead over China. China's Foreign Ministry described the warnings as "fear mongering."

Altman told Fortune in an interview published Saturday that OpenAI would not go public in 2026, saying the current safety environment made it the wrong time. SoftBank Group stock lost 13% in Tokyo on Monday, and South Korean chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each declined more than 4% in Seoul as markets reacted to the weekend's statements.

Tesla $TSLA set an October 1 reveal date for its second-generation Roadster, posting "Go for launch" on X $TWTR alongside a graphic displaying "10.01." CEO Elon Musk later replied to the post, writing, "New Tesla Roadster Unveil 10.01."

The demonstration is expected to take place at SpaceX's rocket test facility in McGregor, Texas, according to Reuters. The graphic accompanying Tesla 's post appears to reference the cold gas thrusters developed by SpaceX that are associated with the vehicle, according to TechCrunch.

Tesla debuted the next-generation Roadster in November 2017, with the company anticipating at the time that customers would receive vehicles starting in 2020. Years of setbacks have followed. According to Reuters, Tesla scrapped a design rooted in Model S Plaid underpinnings and pivoted to an entirely new carbon fiber architecture for the Roadster.

The limited-edition model Tesla intends to demonstrate in Texas would not be road-legal and may carry a price tag in the hundreds of thousands of dollars or higher. The thrusters produce enough noise to risk hearing injury, so the car will run without anyone inside while onlookers are positioned several hundred yards away. Elon Musk has told staff that the demonstration will be difficult to execute and could go wrong.

The original concept for the demonstration was more ambitious. Earlier plans had the car launching up a magnetized ramp, flipping inverted, recovering, and sustaining flight — ambitions that have since been reduced. "We started off thinking we were almost making an aircraft and ended up with something closer to hovering," one person with knowledge of the program said.

According to TechCrunch, Musk has indicated that manufacturing of the Roadster remains at least a year to a year and a half away, regardless of what the October event shows.

The Roadster announcement follows Tesla 's introduction of rides in its two-seater Cybercab in limited areas of Austin, Texas, according to Reuters. Musk has described the Cybercab as a cornerstone of his broader vision for Tesla 's future in autonomous transportation.

President Donald Trump announced plans to remove the 10% U.S. tariff on Irish whiskey on Sunday, making the surprise declaration at the trophy ceremony for the Irish Open golf tournament at his Trump International Golf Links course in Doonbeg, Ireland.

Trump said Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, Irish Open winner Shane Lowry, and others had pressed him on the issue. "Everybody's been bugging me," Trump said. "And I said, 'On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off.'" The crowd responded with cheers and whistles.

Irish whiskey currently falls under the 10% baseline tariff applied to most E.U. imports under Trump, down from the 15% rate that was in place before July. America accounts for more Irish whiskey sales than any other country — the Irish Whiskey Association puts 2024 U.S. volume at approximately 5.5 million cases, or around one in every three bottles sold globally, according to the Wall Street Journal. The association has put the annual value of those U.S. exports at €450 million, or about $520 million, the Journal reported.

The announcement mirrors a concession Trump made earlier this year after King Charles III and Queen Camilla visited the White House. Trump said on April 30 that he would remove tariffs on U.K. whiskey — which includes Scotch and spirits made in Northern Ireland — attributing the decision to the royal couple's visit. That zero-tariff policy came into effect on July 24, creating a disparity with Ireland that the Irish Whiskey Association had flagged in May, calling for equal treatment.

No timeline was provided for when the tariff removal would take effect. The Journal noted that it received no reply from the White House when seeking comment on the announcement.

The Distilled Spirits Council of the United States CEO Chris Swonger praised the move as "another positive step toward reducing barriers to spirits trade," adding that retailers, restaurants, and consumers would benefit heading into the holiday season.

Simon Harris, who serves as Ireland's deputy prime minister and minister of finance, welcomed the news in a statement carried by CNN, calling it "a welcome announcement of economic significance" that "reflects the very positive engagement we've had with the U.S. administration on tariffs over the 18 months."

Trump's trip to Ireland also included meetings with Martin and Irish President Catherine Connolly, as well as comments that drew attention across Europe, where his administration has been reshaping trade relationships with major partners including France.

President Donald Trump endorsed the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act on Sunday as Senate Republicans published what they called the legislation's final text, even as banks and the crypto industry remained at odds over stablecoin provisions ahead of a Tuesday procedural vote.

Senators Cynthia Lummis, John Boozman, and Tim Scott said the updated text incorporates 126 substantive changes requested by Democrats, including ethics language drawn from a proposal by Senators Thom Tillis and Ruben Gallego. Trump agreed to ethics restrictions that would cover the president, vice president, members of Congress, judges, and their spouses, the senators said. The new version also gives the Treasury secretary authority to restrict stablecoin rewards if deposit outflows from community banks reach a substantial level — a measure designed as an emergency brake for community lenders.

"After a year of intense daily bipartisan negotiations, this bill is ready," Senator Lummis said in a statement. "Democrats got what they wanted; now they need to take yes for an answer."

Tuesday's vote is a procedural cloture motion to open floor debate on the legislation. With Republicans occupying 53 Senate seats, the party would need at least seven Democrats or independents to cross over and supply the 60 votes required, according to The Block $SQ.

The banking industry has been the bill's most persistent opponent. A Thursday letter addressed to Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer bore the signatures of the American Bankers Association and close to 80 allied banking organizations, pressing the chamber to impose stricter stablecoin rules, according to CNBC. The coalition argued that existing bill language barring stablecoin interest, yield, and rewards falls short and must be reinforced to safeguard the deposit base that community banks rely on.

"We remain optimistic that the Senate will ultimately consider an improved Clarity Act that embraces innovation without undermining the economy," Brooke Ybarra, senior vice president for innovation and strategy at the American Bankers Association, said in a statement to CNBC.

While some Democrats also remain opposed, a Democratic aide told CNBC that the Tuesday cloture vote could still draw sufficient Democratic support to advance the bill, pointing to Thune's framing of it as a "free vote" — a procedural step that would leave room for additional amendments and another round of voting before any final passage.

The bill left Washington without a vote before Congress's August recess, with Senator Lummis warning at the time that failure to pass it this Congress would delay the legislation until 2030. The Senate's tentative schedule shows a state work period beginning October 5, leaving only a narrow window for further action, according to The Block .

Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google $GOOGL have been holding discussions about creating a shared AI industry standards body, with representatives from the three companies meeting on a working-group basis since at least July, according to The Information. The group met as recently as last week, one person familiar with the matter told the outlet.

Those talks were already underway before Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published his Saturday essay urging coordination on AI testing and auditing, and before a former Anthropic researcher publicly quit, citing concerns that leading AI companies were failing to act responsibly, according to CNN. The discussions are ongoing with or without the support of the Trump administration, CNN reported.

The catalyst for the talks was a July essay by Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis, who proposed a U.S.-led standards body modeled on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which polices Wall Street under Securities and Exchange Commission oversight. In Hassabis's vision, the organization would evaluate advanced AI models prior to their release and operate as a public-private partnership, drawing its funding from industry while employing independent technical experts.

At a companywide town hall earlier last week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told employees he was in favor of establishing a testing and auditing body for the AI industry, though he felt major labs would need to create one independently of government support, according to The Information. Altman acknowledged that industry-wide agreement remained elusive and that certain companies were resistant, but said he saw direct collaboration with peer laboratories as the most viable route.

At a briefing earlier this month, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki said the company had been talking "to some external organizations about potential concrete standards we could put in place" and would have more to share "in the next months," CNN reported.

Not everyone supports the effort. Meta $META CEO Mark Zuckerberg expressed concerns about plans for a national AI regulator in an August phone call with President Donald Trump, according to The Information, citing Politico. The Information also reported that a White House draft executive order aimed at establishing such a body lost momentum and was effectively shelved after it could not secure sufficient backing inside the Trump administration before summer ended.

House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN on Sunday there is little consensus among the companies on what standards and guardrails should look like. "There's no consensus among them," Johnson said. "So this has to be a partnership with the industry itself, with the corporations that are doing this and with the policy and lawmakers."

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez offered a pointed critique, warning on X $TWTR that letting the biggest AI companies jointly set rules risked putting smaller competitors at a disadvantage. "Great ideas here from the cartel," Gomez wrote, according to The Information.

Google , OpenAI, and Anthropic did not provide comment; their representatives either declined or failed to respond to CNN's inquiries.

text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has weighed in on the debate around slowing AI development, agreeing with the need for deliberate pacing but also issuing a wake-up call to industry leaders including Dario Amodei and Sam Altman. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Nadella stressed that any pursuit of superintelligence must be grounded in the principle that AI should hep humanity and also remain under human control. text:
Washington, DC [US], September 14 (ANI): The debate ignited by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei who advocated for a slowdown in AI development or risk losing control continues to engage the Tech Industry. After OpenAI's Sam Altman, Tesla's Elon Musk and Google's Demis Hassabis backed calls for slowing the pace down, Microsoft boss Satya Nadella indicated his support for embedded evaluators in AI systems, a suggestion also mooted by Amodei and Altman.

The Microsoft Chairman and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) said that advanced artificial intelligence systems must remain strictly under human supervision while creators pursue measured progress to guarantee safety.

Writing in a post on X, Nadella stated, 'Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing.'

https://x.com/satyanadella/status/2099220712024408084?s=20

He emphasised the need to accelerate and spread the advantages of artificial intelligence so they are diffused broadly across countries, communities, and companies, noting that this requires a frontier ecosystem in which 'both closed and open-source models can thrive.'

Nadella also asserted that commercial enterprises must maintain complete command over their unique and tacit knowledge, maintaining that every organisation 'should be able to build its own continuous learning loop/hill climbing machine, without becoming dependent on any one model provider, and have the ability to embed its own knowledge into models and weights they control.'

Welcoming the research, focus, and 'deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal,' Nadella expressed support for ideas like 'embedded evaluators' and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this 'more than just talk.'

Furthermore, he warned that governance 'cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia.'

Detailing Microsoft's approach, Nadella highlighted 'broad access and choice at every layer of the AI stack; enterprise control of learning loops and models; and the 'Code of Conduct' that underlies our own first-party MAI models that we'll publish tomorrow for public consultation.'

Earlier in an essay, Amodei elaborated on his stance, stating, 'I have worked on AI for the last twelve years because I believe it could dramatically raise the quality of human life. I've written often about these incredible benefits: I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5-10 years, greatly accelerate economic growth rates, create a world of abundance and empowerment, and usher in a renaissance of democracy and freedom. But like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious. I've written a lot about them too. They include the risk of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption. A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute.'

Amodei warned that unchecked model development could outrun human ability to control such systems, pointing to an incident at OpenAI and Hugging Face where a swarm of agents staged cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack, noting that such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet.

Outlining his strategy to address these concerns, Amodei's three-part plan involves companies committing to giving ongoing, employee-like access to a team of embedded third-party evaluators to verify safety measures, coordinating to establish common safety standards alongside limits on the rate of unchecked progress, and achieving global coordination. He also called for the United States and other democratic governments to coordinate with authoritarian governments while taking the challenges of verifying compliance seriously.

The flurry in the artificial intelligence sector follows an announcement by Jacob Coxon, a researcher associated with Anthropic, who publicly declared he was quitting the industry over fears that the company and its competitors were racing to build systems they would be unable to control. (ANI)

text:
The format, which Digiday has viewed via video and verified, allows advertisers to attach a branded business agent to an ad. When a user clicks the ad’s call-to-action button, which will be a message such as “Chat to us”, they are taken to a branded chat within ChatGPT, where they can interact with the brand’s AI agent.

It’s an early iteration of what OpenAI has described as AI-native advertising — specifically ads designed around the way people interact with AI assistants. The forma, moves beyond the basic ad format that OpenAI currently serves underneath ChatGPT responses to users on its free and Go plans. Instead, the new AI-native ad itself becomes an entry point into a conversation with the brand’s AI agent.

During Goldman Sachs’ Communacopia and Technology Conference in San Francisco on Sept. 8, OpenAI’s CFO Sarah Friar said the current ads under ChatGPT responses are the “basic starting point”, and added that the company is already seeing “early indications” of what a more AI-native ad format could look like.

“This is all before we’ve really launched a format that feels truly endemic to AI,” she said.

While it’s unclear just how many advertisers have had access to this format, Wayfair is trialing it, per a screenshot of the ad viewed by Digiday.

“This is similar to Meta Ads that send people to WhatsApp,” said Farhad Divecha, group CEO of Accuracast. “It’s a way to open lines of communication with prospects, and then advertisers can qualify the ones who need to talk to customer services and sales reps or be directed to the correct page to make a purchase.”

Seven months in, ads in ChatGPT are still promising, still unproven

The launch comes as advertisers are still determining the value of ChatGPT as an ad platform. Until now, each time Digiday has checked in with advertisers that are participating in ChatGPT ads, the consensus has been it’s promising, but still early to make any firm conclusions about its role on a media plan. Until that changes, and a better return can be achieved on ChatGPT ads, investment in the platform will remain relatively lean, within incremental or experimental budgets.

“It makes sense that OpenAI is opening up their ad products,” said Zeno Group’s svp paid media Shamsul Chowdhury. “While they’ve been a hot new platform for advertisers, the ROI just hasn’t been there for the most part.”

The new format could offer OpenAI a way to address that problem by giving advertisers something more akin to an in-platform shopping experience. But it also raises a question, particularly for retailers, over whether there’s a benefit to keeping a potential customer inside ChatGPT rather than sending them to their own site?

“Retailers want to get user data through their owned sites, but they know the consumer journey can happen anywhere and they need to vie for those eyeballs and dollars,” Chowdhury said.

The timing also plays a part as the holiday shopping season approaches, and advertisers ready themselves for the most important quarter of the year. With many facing rising costs and flat returns on platforms such as Google and Meta, Chowdhury said OpenAI could become an alternative channel for some of that spending, provided the agent experience is seamless.

“That’s the big ‘if’,” he said.

Every major ad platform has a signature format that came to define it and, in turn, shapes how advertising worked during that era. Google had the text link ad that turned search into an auction. Facebook had the News Feed ad that made social scrolling monetizable. Tiktok had the in-feed video that blurred content and commercial. OpenAI is now searching for its own version of that, a format native to conversation rather than scroll or search, and this agent-to-agent chat may be an early attempt at it.

OpenAI did not respond to Digiday’s request for comment.

text:
On August 13, OPKO Health (NASDAQ:OPK) expanded its financing relationship with HealthCare Royalty, a business of KKR, issuing an additional $125 million in senior secured notes secured by the royalty stream tied to mazdutide, the GLP-1 drug OPKO licensed to Eli Lilly and now collects royalties on in China. The notes mature in 2044, matching the maturity of OPKO's original HCRx notes, and hand the company fresh capital without selling a single new share.

Cash Without Giving Up The Upside

The structure is the interesting part. Total payments under the expanded deal are capped at 1.5 times the amount OPKO actually receives, and once that cap is hit, OPKO keeps the future royalty economics on that stream for itself. Mazdutide is commercialized in China by Innovent Biologics, and OPKO earns royalties on those sales through its Eli Lilly license, having recorded its first mazdutide royalty revenue in 2025 after the drug's China launch. CEO Phillip Frost called mazdutide "a promising opportunity in China" within OPKO's partnered portfolio.

The rest of the business is also trending in the right direction. On July 27, OPKO reported second-quarter revenue of $163.5 million, up from $156.8 million a year earlier, and a net loss of $8.4 million, or a penny a share, a sharp improvement from the $148.4 million loss in the same 2025 quarter. IP and other revenue jumped to $46.1 million from $15 million, helped by $29.4 million tied to an amended Nicoya agreement covering Rayaldee's rollout in China, alongside a growing NGENLA profit share and combined Eli Lilly and Regeneron revenue of $4.3 million. Behind that, OPKO's ModeX unit kept multiple antibody programs moving through early clinical trials.

Where The Growth Isn't

The diagnostics segment tells a different story. Revenue there fell to $74.5 million in the second quarter from $101.1 million a year earlier, largely because OPKO sold its oncology assets to Labcorp in September 2025. That segment only turned a profit this quarter because of an $18.1 million earnout tied to that same sale, not from underlying demand. Revenue tied to OPKO's BARDA contract also slipped to $5.0 million from $6.5 million a year ago.

The mazdutide notes deal cuts both ways, too. Financing against a royalty stream that only began generating revenue in 2025 means OPKO is trading a still-young income source for cash now, and until the 1.5 times cap is repaid, a meaningful share of that stream's near-term value belongs to HealthCare Royalty rather than OPKO. Meanwhile, the company kept buying back stock, spending $13.2 million on repurchases in the quarter, even while it was still posting a net loss, with cash and marketable securities totaling $314.4 million as of June 30.

text:
SoftBank Group secured an $11.87 billion loan to support its investment in U.S. artificial intelligence firm OpenAI, people familiar with the matter said, up from its earlier target of $10 billion.

The Japanese conglomerate sealed the two-year facility last week, attracting commitments from around 20 banks, said the people, asking not to be identified because they’re not authorized to speak publicly.

Softbank declined to comment.

The financing comes as some executives are now voicing the need to slow the pace of AI development due to escalating risks from the technology. OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman said in an interview with Fortune that his company wouldn’t proceed with a public offering this year as it addresses safety-related concerns.

SoftBank shares tumbled as much as 13% Monday, the most since July 17.

The latest borrowing would add to SoftBank’s wave of recent debt financing activities tied to its bet on OpenAI. That includes a $10 billion margin loan backed by its OpenAI stake and a potential bond sale of as much as $20 billion, despite concerns about growing credit risks in the artificial intelligence sector.

SoftBank said last week that it would repay the balance of a $40 billion loan it obtained earlier this year to finance its investment in OpenAI. The company plans to pay down the $25.9 billion it owes on Sept. 15, according to a statement. The non-collateralized borrowing was due to mature in March next year.

Meanwhile, SoftBank is set to hold meetings with investors in New York this week to sound out interest for the potential U.S. dollar junk-bond sale. It is considering raising $10 billion to $20 billion from the bond offering, people familiar with the matter said last month.

SoftBank, founded and led by billionaire Masayoshi Son, is slated to invest close to $65 billion in OpenAI by October. The company has already raised the equivalent of about $37 billion so far this year from offshore and domestic bond sales and loans, including the latest facility, according to Bloomberg-compiled data.

INDIANAPOLIS, Sept. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE: LLY) today announced the successful completion of its acquisition of AtaiBeckley Inc. AtaiBeckley is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing rapid-acting neuroplastogens for mental health conditions, including BPL-003, its lead investigational program for treatment-resistant depression.

"Treatment-resistant depression persists even after multiple treatment attempts, leaving millions of people still searching for relief," said Carole Ho, Lilly executive vice president and president, Lilly Neuroscience. "AtaiBeckley's neuroplastogens have the potential to open a new paradigm of treatment, with rapid-acting therapeutics designed to move away from chronic dosing. It's the innovation this field needs, and we are committed to advancing them for patients who need more options."

The transaction was approved by AtaiBeckley shareholders at a special meeting held prior to closing.

About Lilly

Lilly is a medicine company turning science into healing to make life better for people around the world. We've been pioneering life-changing discoveries for 150 years, and today our medicines help tens of millions of people across the globe. Harnessing the power of biotechnology, chemistry and genetic medicine, our scientists are urgently advancing new discoveries to solve some of the world's most significant health challenges: redefining diabetes care; treating obesity and curtailing its most devastating long-term effects; advancing the fight against Alzheimer's disease; providing solutions to some of the most debilitating immune system disorders; and transforming the most difficult-to-treat cancers into manageable diseases. With each step toward a healthier world, we're motivated by one thing: making life better for millions more people. That includes delivering innovative clinical trials that reflect the diversity of our world and working to ensure our medicines are accessible and affordable. Satya Nadella stressed that companies should retain control over their own unique and tacit knowledge amid the AI race.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has joined a growing group of artificial intelligence leaders calling for stronger safeguards and a more deliberate approach to developing increasingly powerful AI systems. Nadella said the pursuit of superintelligence must remain centred on helping humanity and ensuring that AI stays under human control.

AI vs Humanity

In a post on X, Nadella said the development of superintelligence must be guided by a basic principle: AI should help humanity and remain under human control. “Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing," he said.

At the same time, Nadella called for the benefits of AI to be expanded across countries, communities and companies. He said this would require a frontier ecosystem where both closed and open-source models can develop.

Nadella also stressed that companies should retain control over their own unique and tacit knowledge. According to him, every organisation should be able to build its own continuous learning loop or “hill climbing machine" without becoming dependent on a single model provider.

He said companies should also have the ability to embed their own knowledge into models and the weights they control.

‘Deliberate Pacing’ Needed

Nadella said Microsoft supports research, focus and “deliberate pacing" to ensure that alignment is properly built into AI development as a design goal. He also welcomed ideas such as “embedded evaluators" and wider efforts to develop mechanisms that can turn AI safety commitments into practical measures.

He argued that the development of advanced AI cannot be controlled by only a small number of entities. Instead, it should have broad representation across the AI ecosystem, countries and fields, including academia.

“This is the approach we are taking: broad access and choice at every layer of the AI stack; enterprise control of learning loops and models," Nadella said.

He added that Microsoft’s first-party MAI models would also have a “Code of Conduct", which the company would publish the following day for public consultation.

AI Industry Push For Safety

Nadella’s comments broadly align with a growing push within the AI industry for stronger oversight as AI capabilities advance.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently called on AI companies to “pace the frontier", arguing that safety work needs sufficient time to keep up with rapid advances in model capabilities.

Amodei said Anthropic would provide third-party evaluators with ongoing, employee-level access to its systems. The evaluators would verify safety practices, report incidents and assess the alignment of models and training processes.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed the proposal, saying the company also needed to “pace the frontier". He said independent evaluators with employee-like access were a good approach.

Elon Musk also endorsed Amodei’s position, while Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis said the direction was correct, although details still needed to be worked out.

The “AI vs Humanity" debate has sharpened in 2025–26 around two opposing views: whether advanced AI could become an existential risk threatening human survival or civilisation, or whether it should be treated as a transformative tool capable of addressing humanity’s hardest problems if it is governed properly.

Washington: The debate ignited by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei who advocated for a slowdown in Al development or risk losing control continues to engage the Tech Industry. After OpenAl's Sam Altman, Tesla's Elon Musk and Google's Demis Hassabis backed calls for slowing the pace down, Microsoft boss Satya Nadella indicated his support for embedded evaluators in Al systems, a suggestion also mooted by Amodei and Altman.

The Microsoft Chairman and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) said that advanced artificial intelligence systems must remain strictly under human supervision while creators pursue measured progress to guarantee safety.

Writing in a post on X, Nadella stated, "Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the Al we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing."

He emphasised the need to accelerate and spread the advantages of artificial intelligence so they are diffused broadly across countries, communities, and companies, noting that this requires a frontier ecosystem in which "both closed and open-source models can thrive."

Nadella also asserted that commercial enterprises must maintain complete command over their unique and tacit knowledge, maintaining that every organisation "should be able to build its own continuous learning loop/hill climbing machine, without becoming dependent on any one model provider, and have the ability to embed its own knowledge into models and weights they control."

Welcoming the research, focus, and "deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal," Nadella expressed support for ideas like "embedded evaluators" and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this "more than just talk."

Furthermore, he warned that governance "cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia."

Detailing Microsoft's approach, Nadella highlighted "broad access and choice at every layer of the Al stack; enterprise control of learning loops and models; and the 'Code of Conduct' that underlies our own first-party ΜΑΙ models that we'll publish tomorrow for public consultation."

Earlier in an essay, Amodei elaborated on his stance, stating, "I have worked on Al for the last twelve years because I believe it could dramatically raise the quality of human life. I've written often about these incredible benefits: I believe that Al could cure most major diseases in the next 5-10 years, greatly accelerate economic growth rates, create a world of abundance and empowerment, and usher in a renaissance of democracy and freedom. But like many technologies before it, Al brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious. I've written a lot about them too. They include the risk of losing control of Al systems, misuse of Al for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption. A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute."

Outlining his strategy to address these concerns, Amodei's three-part plan involves companies committing to giving ongoing, employee-like access to a team of embedded third-party evaluators to verify safety measures, coordinating to establish common safety standards alongside limits on the rate of unchecked progress, and achieving global coordination. He also called for the United States and other democratic governments to coordinate with authoritarian governments while taking the challenges of verifying compliance seriously.

The flurry in the artificial intelligence sector follows an announcement by Jacob Coxon, a researcher associated with Anthropic, who publicly declared he was quitting the industry over fears that the company and its competitors were racing to build systems they would be unable to control.

OpenAI will not go public this year, CEO Sam Altman said in an interview released Saturday, delaying one of the most anticipated stock market debuts in Silicon Valley as the artificial intelligence industry faces growing scrutiny over safety.

Altman told Fortune that taking the San Francisco company public now would be the wrong move while OpenAI and other major developers work through questions about how quickly to build more powerful systems.

HPE has raised its fiscal 2026 target for Networks for AI orders to between $2.5 billion and $3 billion, compared with an earlier target of $1.5 billion. Cross pointed to demand across routing and switching products, including the PTX router, MX router and QFX platform.

She said the company sees particular opportunity in routing infrastructure used to connect AI data centers. Cross also cited HPE's direct liquid-cooled QFX switch, which she said is a 100% direct liquid-cooled Tomahawk 6 top-of-rack switch and reached the market at least six months ahead of competing products.

Oracle Deal and Juniper Integration

Cross discussed HPE's previously announced Oracle AI data-center opportunity, describing it as a competitive win involving PTX, MX and QFX products. She said Oracle was attracted by the liquid-cooled switch, HPE's broader scale and its financial-services and leasing capabilities.

The deal serves as a proof point that HPE can compete in AI data-center networking, Cross said, adding that the company is speaking with other market participants about similar opportunities.

HPE expects its combination with Juniper Networks to expand the addressable market for networking products in enterprise and hyperscale accounts. Cross said HPE combined its sales force in January and plans to hold a "Partner Day One" on Nov. 1, when partners will be able to sell both product portfolios.

In campus and branch networking, Cross said HPE recorded low-teens order growth and 8% revenue growth, supported by a Wi-Fi 7 refresh cycle and customer interest in Juniper's Mist technology. She said the company plans to converge the Aruba and Mist offerings over time while seeking to maintain satisfaction among both customer bases.

For fiscal 2027, HPE has raised its networking growth outlook to 14% to 17%, from 8% to 12% previously. Cross said the outlook includes some Oracle contribution and modest acceleration in the core business. She attributed expected segment margin expansion into the mid-to-high 20% range primarily to synergies, while saying HPE will continue investing in silicon development, new products and the AMD Helios platform.

AI Servers and Private AI Infrastructure

Cross said HPE intends to participate in AMD Helios through two approaches: supplying full HPE-branded racks containing server and scale-up networking technology, and supplying white-label trays to other server vendors working with AMD. She said the offering could help HPE pursue hyperscale and neocloud opportunities with a stronger margin profile because it incorporates HPE networking intellectual property.

HPE has maintained a selective approach to AI server deals, Cross said, avoiding what she called "empty-calorie revenue" when margins are insufficient. The company reported $2.4 billion in AI server orders during the quarter and nearly $7 billion in backlog, according to the discussion.

Cross also highlighted a $3.5 billion enterprise deal announced after quarter-end, which she described as a hyperscaler purchasing predominantly CPU-based, traditional servers for internal inference use. She said the deal carries traditional server margins and is expected to move through the business relatively quickly.

HPE sees a growing opportunity for customers to deploy private AI infrastructure to control token costs and keep sensitive data within their own environments. Cross said organizations in sectors including retail, technology, banking and pharmaceuticals are considering such deployments. HPE uses its own Private Cloud AI hardware internally for some workloads, she said.

Cross added that sovereign AI demand remains healthy, particularly in Europe, where governments are interested in maintaining cloud infrastructure within national borders for defense, government services and domestic technology development.

HPE will hold a Networking Investor Day in the Bay Area on Sept. 30, where Cross said management plans to provide additional detail on the combined networking business and its strategy.

text:
Boston Scientific Corporation (NYSE:BSX) fell 2.3% in early trading on September 8, 2026, after disclosing that an August 25 cyberattack disrupted manufacturing and shipping. The company stated it is unlikely to meet its previously issued third-quarter and full-year 2026 guidance for net sales and adjusted earnings per share. Though operations have since resumed, the incident is expected to weigh on third-quarter and full-year results. The risk that never gets modelled by Wall Street has just sent one of medtech's best compounders off course.

Not Demand, Not Devices — Downtime

Farapulse, Boston Scientific's pulsed-field-ablation system, still commands a major share of the US atrial-fibrillation market. The incident itself does not appear to reflect a product-quality problem. The lost sales are orders that could not ship. The demand still exists, and the distribution is already back online. It increases the chances of recovery from a stumble. However, Farapulse was already facing competitive pressure before the cyberattack. Boston Scientific had projected flat global electrophysiology growth for the second half of 2026 after lowering its market-share assumptions, so the outage adds another near-term complication rather than causing the existing EP slowdown

The Bear Case Is More Than "Hackers Happen"

Three structural risks complicate the company's recovery. First, a disruption large enough to impair manufacturing and order fulfillment exposes an operational vulnerability that investors may not have fully priced. Second, the warning that Boston Scientific is unlikely to meet its previously issued guidance further resets near-term earnings expectations. Third, the gap between the initial August 25 disclosure and the September 8 financial warning highlights how difficult the ultimate impact was to quantify. Additionally, in a rapidly adopting PFA market, there also exists the subtlest risk of customer retention. Temporary shipping disruption can hand procedures to Medtronic and Johnson & Johnson that may not fully come back.

Hedge Fund Positioning

Institutional positioning had already begun to ease before the disclosure. Insider Monkey records 99 hedge funds holding BSX shares in the second quarter of 2026, down from 106 in the prior quarter. Short interest remains low at 1.9% of the float, indicating that the current selling reflects portfolio adjustments rather than coordinated short positioning.

Bottom Line

The franchise is intact, and the cause behind the guidance cut is exogenous, making Boston Scientific Corporation (NYSE:BSX) one of the better recovery candidates. For investors who remain constructive on the long-term PFA franchise, the selloff could create a recovery setup, but near-term visibility remains unusually weak. However, realized operational risks often lead to valuation multiple compression. Wait for the third-quarter results. A stronger entry case would depend on stabilized order rates and evidence that electrophysiology market share remains intact.

text:
The production paradigm within the pharmaceutical industry is witnessing significant changes. There is a trend among pharmaceutical companies of using contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs) for process development, clinical production, manufacturing, formulation, and fill-finish services. Outsourcing processes which were previously perceived as cost-cutting strategies have transformed into something more than that as a result of advancements in medicine and redesigning of supply chains.

Several examples illustrate the trend. As reported in July 2026, Lonza enhanced a strategic partnership with a major US biopharmaceutical company through the addition of two commercial biologics programs, with the entire deal potentially amounting to billions of Swiss francs.

In addition to the foregoing, Samsung Biologics offered a CHF 1.46 billion takeover of PolyPeptide- CDMO focused on peptides in July 2026. With the deal, Samsung will expand its portfolio of products from antibodies to peptide-based active pharmaceutical ingredients, diversifying its manufacturing facilities in the US, Europe, and India.

The examples indicate the change in role of CDMOs from traditional outsourcing into technological strategic partnerships with a wide range of products such as biologics, peptides, advanced therapies, and other complex drugs.

Pharma's manufacturing model is changing

The pharmaceutical manufacturing model is shifting from traditional in-house production toward integrated partnerships with contract development and manufacturing organisations (CDMOs). The global pharmaceutical CDMO market was valued at around US$197 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach approximately US$369 billion by 2034, representing a CAGR of about 7.1%. The biologics-focused CDMO segment is also expected to expand rapidly, reflecting the growing complexity of drug pipelines.

Biologics, peptides, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), targeted protein degraders and cell and gene therapies increasingly require specialised facilities, advanced analytical systems and high-containment manufacturing. For smaller and virtual biotechnology companies, outsourcing provides access to these capabilities without the enormous capital investment required to build them internally.

The CDMO relationship is consequently becoming broader. Companies are increasingly seeking partners that can provide process and formulation development, analytical testing, clinical manufacturing, commercial production, sterile fill-finish, packaging and device assembly under an integrated model. Industry discussions have highlighted growing demand for single-source providers that can reduce technology transfers, simplify coordination and improve accountability.

Investment is following this trend. PCI Pharma Services has committed more than US$365 million to new and expanded facilities across North America and Europe, including a 545,000-square-foot facility in Illinois. The investment targets complex injectable products, packaging, storage and drug-device combination products.

The shift signals a fundamental change: CDMOs are evolving from outsourced manufacturers into strategic partners capable of supporting complex medicines from early development through commercialisation.

Why Is This Happening Right Now?

The current wave of CDMO activity is being driven by several forces converging at the same time, reshaping how pharmaceutical companies approach manufacturing, investment and outsourcing.

Pressure to Bring Production Closer to Home

Governments and pharmaceutical companies are placing greater emphasis on domestic manufacturing to strengthen medicine supply chains and reduce dependence on overseas production. Policy initiatives such as the BIOSECURE Act are adding further pressure for companies to reconsider where and with whom critical pharmaceutical manufacturing is carried out.

Uncertainty Over Trade and Tariffs

Changing tariff policies are prompting pharmaceutical companies to reassess global manufacturing footprints. Some drugmakers are considering whether certain facilities are more efficiently operated by specialised CDMOs, while others are restructuring networks to increase US-based production.

More Favourable Financing Conditions

Biopharma faced a difficult financing environment between 2022 and 2024, when higher interest rates put pressure on valuations and investment activity. Improving credit conditions are now giving potential buyers greater financial flexibility, encouraging renewed interest in acquisitions and strategic investments.

A Move Toward Specialisation

The previous CDMO expansion cycle focused heavily on building broad, end-to-end capabilities. The emerging model is more targeted, with companies concentrating on specialised areas such as biologics, peptides, ADCs, high-potency drugs and advanced manufacturing technologies. The emphasis is increasingly on depth of expertise rather than simply offering the widest possible range of services.

Complex medicines are driving the next wave

There is an evolution taking place in the pipeline of the pharmaceutical industry and, in turn, in the requirements that pharma companies have for contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs). There are evolving advanced biological drugs, peptides, oligonucleotides, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), targeted protein degraders (TPDs), cell and gene therapies, and sterile injectables, which are no longer limited to niche indications but are fast turning into important pharmaceutical areas of development. Consequently, there is an increasing demand for CDMOs with special technologies and science as well as controlled manufacturing processes.

The global biologics CDMO market had a market valuation of approximately US$32.2 billion in 2025, which is expected to grow to approximately US$103.1 billion by 2035 at a CAGR of 12.48% during the forecast period 2026-2035.

These therapies can require sophisticated analytical testing, functional assays, high-potency containment and precise dose control. Some products are also highly sensitive to environmental conditions, increasing the need for specialised formulation, lyophilisation and packaging technologies.

Meanwhile, rising demand for GLP-1 medicines and other injectable therapies is strengthening the need for sterile manufacturing and drug-device capabilities. Pharmaceutical companies are consequently looking beyond production capacity when selecting CDMO partners. They increasingly want providers capable of supporting development, scale-up, validation and commercial manufacturing while maintaining stringent regulatory and quality standards.

The industry is therefore moving from capacity-driven outsourcing toward expertise-driven partnerships, where technical capability, reliability and regulatory performance increasingly determine competitiveness.

Billions are moving into manufacturing capacity

The CDMO industry is attracting major investments as pharmaceutical companies seek reliable capacity for biologics, injectables, peptides and specialised APIs. Recent developments across the US and India highlight how the sector is moving toward technology-intensive and regionally diversified manufacturing.

Eli Lilly and Resilience announced a US$750 million investment to expand production of Lilly's injectable KwikPen devices at a Resilience facility in Ohio. The project is expected to create at least 400 jobs, strengthening US-based manufacturing for diabetes and obesity medicines.

Evonik is investing US$100 million over five years to modernise its Tippecanoe Laboratories in Indiana. The upgrade will strengthen high-potency API manufacturing and expand the site's capabilities for specialised pharmaceutical production.

India is also becoming an important destination for CDMO investment. TheraNym Biologics, an Aurobindo Pharma subsidiary, plans to invest around US$150-175 million in a new mammalian biologics facility in Hyderabad, with approximately 60,000 litres of bioreactor capacity.

Meanwhile, Neuland Laboratories is developing a commercial-scale peptide facility in Telangana with 6,370 litres of peptide synthesis capacity and approximately US$30 million in firm customer commitments.

Hovione has also invested US$100 million in expanding its New Jersey operations, including spray-drying capabilities.

Together, these projects show that CDMO competition is increasingly centred on specialised technology, regional supply, capacity flexibility and long-term customer relationships, rather than manufacturing volume alone.

AI & Digital Manufacturing

Artificial intelligence and digital technologies are becoming increasingly important across CDMO operations, supporting manufacturers improve efficiency, quality and decision-making. During process development, AI and machine-learning tools can analyse experimental data and identify promising production conditions, potentially reducing development timelines by 30-50%. Companies are also exploring AI for predictive quality control, using production data to identify potential deviations early and allow corrective action before batches fail. This is particularly valuable for biologics, where a failed batch can result in losses estimated at US$500,000 to US$5 million. AI is also being applied to supply-chain planning, supporting CDMOs forecast demand, manage inventories and optimise capacity across multiple facilities. Another emerging technology is the digital twin, which creates a virtual representation of a manufacturing process. It can help companies test process changes, predict scale-up challenges and troubleshoot operations digitally before making costly physical changes.

Challenges

Technology transfer remains a major challenge for CDMOs because a process that performs successfully at laboratory scale may behave differently during commercial production. Differences in equipment, batch size, raw materials and operating conditions can affect quality, consistency and timelines. As outsourcing expands, effective technology transfer is therefore becoming critical to successful drug manufacturing. Digital manufacturing systems, advanced process analytics and real-time data sharing can help reduce transfer risks and improve process control. At the same time, rapid investment in new CDMO facilities raises concerns about potential overcapacity, particularly if pharmaceutical demand or biotechnology funding slows. This risk is especially relevant to fast-growing areas such as peptides and GLP-1 medicines, where several companies are expanding simultaneously. CDMOs with long-term contracts, diversified customers, specialised technologies, strong regulatory capabilities and efficient facilities are expected to remain best positioned.

The global pharmaceutical outsourcing industry is entering a more sophisticated era, driven by specialised technology, quality, regulatory expertise, manufacturing flexibility and diversified supply chains. Recent developments, including Samsung Biologics’ US manufacturing expansion, India’s growing capabilities in complex pharmaceuticals, and rising demand for peptides and advanced therapies, highlight this transformation. Future industry leaders will not simply be those with the largest manufacturing capacities, but companies that combine scale with specialised expertise, maintain exceptional quality and integrate closely with customers’ development and commercial strategies. Rival OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) CEO Sam Altman followed up on Amodei's piece, which he published Saturday morning, via a post on X saying that he agrees with Anthropic's chief executive.

The announcements come after two AI researchers posted about the dangers of advanced frontier AI models.

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt," he wrote. "If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger."

Anthropic's Alignment Science Lead, Evan Hubinger, then replied to Coxon's post saying the former Anthropic worker is correct and that he believes there is a greater-than-10 % chance that the technology could "kill all humans."

The posts set off alarm bells from Silicon Valley to Washington, DC over the potential dangers posed by the technology.

But President Trump on Sunday pushed back on the safety concerns, saying that "We're leading China in ​AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins," Reuters reported.

While he said he is open to guardrails on AI, he also said that "very negative forces" are "bringing up things that won't happen."

The AI warnings come after a summer of revelations from the industry in which Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta (META) reported that their respective models attempted to or successfully hacked into outside organizations' systems.

AI researchers and CEOs have repeatedly expressed concerns that the technology could cause societal upheaval, including major job losses.

The latest fears come amid talk of recursive self-improvement, or AI that is so advanced it can develop better AI models on its own.

In his essay, Amodei says AI using recursive self-improvement, "could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all."

name: OpenAI
title: Anthropic CEO outlines plan to slow AI development | TechCrunch
description:
We’ve been seeing increasingly dire warnings from AI researchers about the dangers of artificial intelligence, and even comments from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that it may be time to “pace” AI development.
In a new blog post, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei not only echoed the call to “pace the frontier,” but also outlined three broad strategies for doing so.
And he said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing” to one of them, with Altman chiming in to say OpenAI will follow suit.
(OpenAI was recently criticized for not reporting an incident where its AI agents took over a German wiki forum.)
Industry critics have also been skeptical about these apocalyptic AI warnings, suggesting that they’re a distraction from the harm that the technology is already causing.
text:
We’ve been seeing increasingly dire warnings from AI researchers about the dangers of artificial intelligence, and even comments from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that it may be time to “pace” AI development. But what would that actually look like?

In a new blog post, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei not only echoed the call to “pace the frontier,” but also outlined three broad strategies for doing so. And he said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing” to one of them, with Altman chiming in to say OpenAI will follow suit.

The debate over AI safety and alignment intensified this week after researcher Jacob Coxon wrote that he’s resigning from Anthropic over concerns that the leading AI companies are “gambling with our lives” while the people building the technology “earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” a claim repeated by others at Anthropic.

Amodei’s post doesn’t didn’t explicitly mention Coxon’s resignation or his concerns, but the CEO wrote that two things convinced him it’s time to take a more cautious approach to AI development: the OpenAI-HuggingFace hack, and the fact that “AI has been advancing drastically faster” in recent months, particularly with its “growing ability to build the next generation of AI.”

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

Other AI executives seem to have reacted positively to Amodei’s post, with Altman writing, “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.” And SpaceX CEO Elon Musk posted, “Dario is right.”

Amodei’s proposed first step would involve “embedded evaluators” from third-party organizations like METR — evaluators who can verify that AI companies are actually following their pacing and safety commitments and can also ensure that safety incidents get reported. (OpenAI was recently criticized for not reporting an incident where its AI agents took over a German wiki forum.)

Amodei compared these evaluators to regulators who have been embedded with bank employees, and he said that inviting them in is “something Anthropic is unilaterally committing to (and calls on governments to require other frontier companies to match).” That means giving evaluators company badges, desks, and laptops, and providing access “mostly comparable to what internal risk assessment teams have,” with exceptions when required by law or contracts.

Altman also said this was a “good idea” and said OpenAI would do the same: “We’ll have more to share soon.”

Next, Amodei called for the leading AI companies “within democratic countries” to coordinate “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”

Such coordination might seem unlikely, because these companies are reportedly worried that a coordinated pause could lead to antitrust scrutiny. Amodei alluded to that concern in his post, writing that “for antitrust reasons, it’s helpful for the US government to mediate or at least enable these discussions — they don’t need to participate, but do need to issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations.”

Amodei also acknowledged the specter of Chinese AI dominance that’s often raised an argument against slowing development. But he said that if the US government and tech companies take steps like refusing to sell powerful chips or semiconductor manufacturing equipment to Chinese companies, as well as cracking down on model distillation, they could “slow China’s progress enough to widen America’s lead significantly over the next 3–5 years.”

Lastly, Amodei called for “global coordination,” where the United States and its allies “attempt to coordinate with authoritarian governments, to the extent this is possible.” Amodei said this would mean “cooperation with China,” and he admitted that there are “stark limits on what can be achieved,” but he still suggested there might be opportunities for agreement, even if it’s just “prohibiting certain narrow and obviously dangerous uses of AI, such as using AI for the production of biological weapons or allowing users to do so.”

With Amodei’s past willingness to acknowledge AI’s potential dangers, and with the company’s relative openness to certain forms of regulation, some AI boosters have already criticized him as a doomer whose comments have fed the current AI backlash. In response, Amodei said he’s tried to offer a “balanced” perspective” and argued that the backlash is “fundamentally a crisis of trust,” as people have become skeptical of tech companies, the tech industry, and the government.

Industry critics have also been skeptical about these apocalyptic AI warnings, suggesting that they’re a distraction from the harm that the technology is already causing.

Journalist Brian Merchant, for example, wrote that he has yet to see “a credible, step-by-step documentation of how exactly AI might move from self-recursively improving AI to killing every single human on the planet”; he also suggested that proposals similar to Amodei’s “would likely only wind up serving Anthropic and OpenAI; it’s what regulatory capture looks like in action.”

In his new post, Amodei wrote that he continues “to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life.”

“My desire to achieve these benefits is undimmed,” he said. “But the benefits will only be achieved if we build the technology in the right way, and — so long as we use the time we gain well — it is worth taking unusually deliberate care to get it right.”

This post has been updated with comments from Sam Altman and Elon Musk.

text:
On September 10, Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) posted record third-quarter revenue of $6.76 billion, up 13% year over year, and raised its full-year revenue and profit targets. Non-GAAP EPS climbed 15% to $6.13, while GAAP EPS rose 11% to $4.62. Buried inside those headline numbers was a sharper story: AI-first ending ARR topped $650 million, growing more than 150% year over year. The same call brought a leadership change, with Anil S. Chakravarthy set to take over as CEO from Shantanu Narayen on December 1. Investors got a lot to digest in one afternoon.

AI Finally Pays For Itself

Adobe's AI tools are no longer just a demo. Firefly ending ARR, which spans the Firefly app and its credit packs, grew 40% quarter over quarter, and the Acrobat AI Assistant doubled its monthly active users over the same three months. Total monthly active users across Adobe's businesses surpassed 1 billion in the quarter, up more than 20% year over year, and creative premium MAU crossed 100 million, up more than 70%. Business professionals and consumers MAU passed 900 million, up more than 25%. That kind of user growth, concentrated in free and freemium tiers, is what feeds the paid AI upgrades now showing up in ARR.

The company backed that growth with cash. Operating cash flow hit a third-quarter record of $2.52 billion, and Adobe bought back roughly 9.5 million shares during the quarter, leaving $24.55 billion still authorized for repurchases. Management raised its full-year revenue target to a range of $26.58 billion to $26.63 billion and its non-GAAP EPS target to $24.45 to $24.50. On the product side, Adobe struck a deal to acquire Topaz Labs, whose AI enhancement models for image and video work would slot directly into Firefly and Creative Cloud. Enterprise demand held up too, with ending ARR growing more than 20% year over year at each of Adobe Experience Manager, Adobe Gen Studio, and Adobe Experience Platform.

Forward Bookings Tell A Slower Story

Not every metric moved as fast. Remaining performance obligations, the backlog of contracted but unrecognized revenue, grew 8% year over year to $22.16 billion, trailing both the 13% revenue growth and the 11.2% growth in total ending ARR. Current RPO grew 9%, also behind the topline. Interim CFO Steven Day flagged a separate issue heading into the fourth quarter: a foreign-exchange headwind that partly offset the benefit of the third-quarter beat when management updated its full-year guidance.

AI-first ARR, for all its 150% growth rate, is still just over $650 million against a total ARR base of $27.50 billion, so it remains a small slice of the business even as it scales. The transition arrives at a pivotal moment too, with Chakravarthy set to take the CEO seat on Dec. 1 just as the company leans harder into an unproven agentic-software strategy, and the Topaz Labs deal still needs to clear regulatory approval before it adds anything to the numbers.
